extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and mass-communication students
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the Hierarchical Influences Model to explain or evaluate how multiple levels (from macro social systems to individual journalists) shape media content; useful for empirical studies of news production and comparative media research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The macro social systems level is the outer-most ring of the model that represent the influences from social systems as a whole. This level focus on how ideological forces shape and influence media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate national/cultural/ideological contexts and structural forces (e.g., political ideologies, legal regimes, cultural norms) that shape media output; commonly employed in cross‑national comparative media studies. Consider how large-scale social values and systemic power relations create constraints or incentives for media content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Social institutional level describes influences coming from larger trans-organizational media field. How media organizations combine into larger institutions that become part of larger structured relationships that compete or depend on each other as powerful social institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess field-level dynamics: ownership structures, inter-organizational relationships, professional associations, market structures, and institutional dependencies or competition. Look at how these trans-organizational forces shape norms, resource flows, and strategic orientations that affect content across organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organization level is distinguished from routines as this level describes larger organizational and occupational context such as organizational policy, occupational roles, and how the media enterprise itself is structured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine organizational policies, editorial lines, management decisions, staffing and occupational roles, business models, and internal hierarchies. Evaluate how organizational-level rules, incentives, and structures (e.g., revenue pressures, ownership interests, editorial guidelines) constrain or direct journalists and content choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The routines level has three sources of routines, which constrain and enable communicators in their work process: audiences, organizations, and suppliers of content. Journalists have developed routines from endless pattern of norms in response to common situations. This level is where gatekeeping (communication) theory is also applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze everyday newsroom practices and procedural norms (e.g., deadlines, sourcing habits, news values, beats, reliance on PR and wire services). Consider the three sources — audience expectations, organizational workflows, and content suppliers — and how they enable or constrain story selection and framing. Apply gatekeeping concepts to see how routine processes filter information into news output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The micro individual level is located at the center of the model. On this level, individual communicator's characteristics, on both personal and professional, influence media content. Individual's innate characteristics such as gender, race, religious and political background influence media content indirectly through shaping personal attitude and values (e.g. ethical values) as well as professional roles and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider journalists' personal attributes, beliefs, values, education, professional socialization, and role conceptions. Assess how individual-level factors (demographics, political/religious views, ethics, professional training) shape decisions about story selection, sourcing, and framing, often mediating higher-level pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media content as dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Hierarchy of Influences' framework treats media content as the dependent variable and five levels of influences as potential independent variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or researching news content, model content outcomes as the product of multiple influence levels rather than as the independent cause. Use multi-level analysis to trace how macro, institutional, organizational, routine, and individual factors each contribute to specific content features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-level interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework 'takes into account the multiple forces that simultaneously impinge on media and suggests how influence at one level may interact with that at another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat levels as isolated: investigate interactions and mediations (e.g., how organizational policy channels social-system pressures into routines, or how individual values moderate the effect of organizational rules). Empirical designs should allow for interaction effects and nested influence relationships.
